
---
title: "Data Handling"
---


## Using Weights


LIS provides two versions of the weights at each level of its data: the **inflated** and the **normalised** ones. At the household level these are `hpopwgt` and `hwgt`, and at the person level `ppopwgt` and `pwgt`. Within each level, both versions come from the same survey weights and differ only in scale.

| | Inflated | Normalised |
|---|---|---|
| **Household level** | `hpopwgt` | `hwgt` |
| **Person level** | `ppopwgt` | `pwgt` |
| **Scale** | Grossed up towards the population | Rescaled to a common scale across datasets |
| **Use for** | Absolute totals (number of households or people) | Shares, means, medians, Gini, poverty rates, and comparisons across datasets |

For ratios and distribution statistics, the scale of the weight cancels out, so the inflated and normalised weights give the same result within one dataset. The **normalised weights** matter when you **compare or pool datasets, because no country counts for more just because it is larger**. Use the inflated weights only when you need real totals, such as the number of poor people.

The level of the file also matters. The household file has one row per household, so the household weight counts households. Many indicators, such as the poverty rate or the Gini of equivalised income, describe **people**. All members of a household share the same equivalised income, so when you work on the household file, each household should count once for each of its members:

$$
\text{person weight} = \texttt{hwgt} \times \texttt{nhhmem}
$$

For example, take household A with 4 members and household B with 1 member, both with `hwgt = 1`. Per household, each counts as 50%. Per person, A counts as 80% and B as 20%. The same logic gives the weights for subgroups, using `nhhmem17` for children and `nhhmem65` for people aged 65 and over.

| Population of interest | File | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Households | Household | `hwgt` |
| Total population | Household | `hwgt * nhhmem` |
| Children (under 18) | Household | `hwgt * nhhmem17` |
| Elderly (65 and over) | Household | `hwgt * nhhmem65` |
| Persons (person-level variables) | Person | `pwgt` |
| Absolute number of households | Household | `hpopwgt` |
| Absolute number of people | Household | `hpopwgt * nhhmem` |
| Absolute number of people | Person | `ppopwgt` |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb

Use the **normalised** weights for rates, shares, distributions and comparisons, and the **inflated** weights for counts. Multiply by `nhhmem` only when you start from the household file and want results for people.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistakes

- **Multiplying a person weight by `nhhmem`.** `pwgt` and `ppopwgt` already count people, so do not multiply them by anything.
- **Using `hwgt * nhhmem` after merging household variables onto the person file.** The person file has one row per person, so each household would be counted `nhhmem` times too often. Use `pwgt` there.
- **Using a normalised weight for an absolute total.** The normalised weights are not scaled to the population, so a sum gives a number that does not match real counts. Use `hpopwgt` or `ppopwgt` instead.
- **Equivalising income but weighting by households.** If you divide income by the square root of `nhhmem` but weight only with `hwgt`, you describe households with equivalised incomes, not the distribution of people.
:::
